passage:
I'm Lokesh, and last month I nearly refused a perfectly good habit before I had even tried it. Baljeet, my team lead, sent a one-line email: "From Monday everyone logs hours in the new tracker. No exceptions." My jaw went tight. I typed a reply about how the old sheet worked fine and how we are not schoolkids.
Before sending, I made tea and asked myself a question: am I against the tracker, or just against being ordered? I opened it. Honestly, it was better. It would end the Friday chaos of chasing everyone's hours.
So I deleted the reply. I used the tracker on Monday and sent Baljeet a separate note asking if the team could suggest fields next month. That part I still wanted to say.

qa.q: What did Baljeet's one-line email say?
qa.a: It said that from Monday everyone logs hours in the new tracker, with no exceptions.

qa.q: What does Lokesh's tight jaw suggest about the first reaction to the email?
qa.a: It suggests irritation at being ordered, as if the freedom to choose was being taken away, before Lokesh had even looked at the tracker.

qa.q: How did Lokesh choose a response deliberately?
qa.a: Lokesh paused, asked whether the objection was to the idea or to being told, judged the tracker on its merits, and kept only the part worth saying: a request for the team's input.

qa.q: How might Baljeet read the two possible replies from Lokesh?
qa.a: The angry reply would likely come across as defiance and start a fight, while the note asking to suggest fields reads as a helpful teammate.

grounding: It shows a young adult who bristles at a rule, asks whether the objection is to the idea or to being told, and chooses a response on purpose.

Coach's notes, Sunday league, week 6
At practice I asked Jaya, my assistant, to tell Deven he would be trying left back this week. Jaya said it plainly, in front of the others. Deven's face changed at once. He folded his arms and said, "I've played striker for six years."
Then I saw something new from him. He walked a few steps away, drank some water, and came back. He asked Jaya, "Is this because I'm bad up front, or because you need someone on the left?" Jaya explained the gap on the left side.
He said, "Okay. I'll try it for two matches, then I want to talk about it." Today he played it properly, no sulking.
Next: I will check in with him after the second match, as he asked, and give changes like this privately.
Uma

qa.a: Deven was asked to try left back.

qa.a: Deven felt hurt and defensive, being told in front of the others to leave the striker role he had played for six years, so his first instinct was to resist.

Omkar said it again today, standing in our kitchen with his arms crossed: "Bro, you need to learn to cook. You can't live on parcel food." I felt that heat in my neck, said "I'll eat what I want," and ordered biryani out of pure spite. Actually ordered it, while he watched.
Eating it, I felt stupid. Because I've wanted to learn dal for months. Aai's dal. I just didn't want it to be his idea.

passage: When Thomas took over the family pepper garden in Wayanad, Noor, the young agriculture officer, came by with a clipboard. "You're spraying too often. Follow the schedule in this leaflet and keep a record, or the cooperative won't buy your pepper this season." Thomas felt his jaw tighten. His father had farmed this land for thirty years without a leaflet. He almost said, "Who asked you?" Instead he walked to the tap and washed his hands slowly. Is it the advice I hate, he asked himself, or being told, by someone younger, on my own land? He read the leaflet that night. The spraying part made sense; the record book was only paperwork. Next morning he phoned Noor. "I'll follow the spray schedule. Can you show me how to fill in the record?"

qa.q: What did Thomas do in the moment that helped him respond well?
qa.a: He walked to the tap and washed his hands slowly, giving himself time to ask whether he disliked the advice or just being told.

passage: At the community sports centre, Darshan was halfway through his squats when the trainer, Harish, called across the floor, "Knees out! You'll wreck your back like that!" Two people turned to look. Darshan felt heat rush to his face. He had been lifting for three years; he didn't need a lecture in front of everyone. He put the bar down harder than necessary. Then he caught himself. Was he angry at the advice, or at being corrected out loud? He watched himself in the mirror and did one slow squat. His knees were caving in. The advice was right. The shouting was what he hated. He finished the set with his knees out, then walked over. "Thanks for the tip. Could you tell me quietly next time?" Harish looked surprised, then nodded. "Deal. Good squat, by the way."

qa.q: What did Harish call across the floor?
qa.a: 'Knees out! You'll wreck your back like that!'

qa.q: Why did Darshan put the bar down harder than necessary?
qa.a: Darshan felt embarrassed and angry at being corrected out loud in front of others after three years of lifting.

qa.q: What did Darshan do that turned the moment around?
qa.a: He checked his form in the mirror, saw the advice was right, used it, and then asked Harish to tell him quietly next time.

qa.q: How might Harish see Darshan's request?
qa.a: Harish might be surprised but willing, realising the shout embarrassed Darshan even though the tip was useful.

Dear Usha,
I owe you a better reply than the one I gave in the corridor yesterday. When you told me I should stop volunteering for every side project, I said, "I can manage my own time, thanks," and walked off. I'm sorry for that.
Last night I asked myself something I've been trying to practise: was I rejecting your idea, or just the feeling of being told? Honestly, it was the second. I hate being told what to do; it makes me want to do the opposite. But when I looked at my calendar, you were right. Three side projects, two late deliveries on my main work, and I'm tired all the time.
So I'm dropping the website redesign and the newsletter, and keeping only the mentoring. Could we check in about it next month?
Thanks for saying it,
Sumit

My name's Vishal, and my manager Lokesh once told me, "You should really take the data course before next quarter." And I felt this heat in my neck. Like, who are you to plan my weekends?

I actually started typing a reply about how busy I was. Then I stopped and asked myself: am I annoyed at the course, or am I annoyed at being told?

Honestly? The course sounded useful. I'd looked at it myself a month earlier. What bothered me was the "you should."

So I went to Lokesh and said, "I'll take it, but I'd like to pick the batch timing." He said sure. I finished it in six weeks, and the heat in my neck was never about the course at all.

Akash, I saw your face when the manager told you to redo the report format. Let me tell you something from when I was twenty-four, in my first job at the port office.
My boss said, "Ramesh, you must file your reports by Thursday noon, not Friday." Just like that, an order. I felt my neck go hot. Who is he to tell me? I'd been planning to file on Friday anyway, but now I wanted to file on Saturday, just to show him.
On the bus home I asked myself a question that has saved me many times since: am I against the idea, or am I just against being told? The truth was, Thursday was better. The ships came in on Fridays, and the reports helped plan them.
So on Thursday at eleven, I filed. My boss nodded. I didn't feel smaller. I felt like I'd chosen it.
So, Akash. Is the new format bad? Or were you just told?

Ten minutes before the client call, Sumit was pasting the last numbers into the slides when Lalremsiami leaned over his desk. "Run the spell-check and read the numbers aloud once. Last time there was a typo in the total."
Sumit felt the bristle rise up his back. He didn't need a checklist; he'd been doing slides for three years. The office was loud with someone's birthday song, and he wanted to snap, "I know."
Instead he took a breath and asked himself the question he'd been practising: is she wrong, or do I just hate being told?
She wasn't wrong. Last month's typo had cost them an awkward apology.
"Fair," he said. He read the numbers aloud under the birthday noise and found one: 1,450 where it should have been 1,540.
"Thanks," he said, fixing it with two minutes to spare. The bristle was still there, a little. But he had chosen what to do with it.

"You should take this weekend off," Irawati said, sliding his laptop shut at the dining table of their Bengaluru flat. "You've worked six weekends in a row."
Ramesh felt the familiar heat in his chest. She's not my boss. He reached to open the laptop again, mostly because she had closed it.
Then he stopped, hand on the lid. This year he had started a habit: when he felt that bristle, he asked himself one question. Do I disagree with this, or do I just not like being told?
He thought about it honestly. His back hurt. He had snapped at his team on Friday. He hadn't called his mother in two weeks.
"I don't like being told," he said slowly. "But you're right."
Irawati laughed. "Both can be true."
He put the laptop in the cupboard and called his mother.
